questions.question: Explain event propagation: capturing, bubbling, and when to stop it.
questions.title: Events Capture Bubble
questions.direct_answer: An event travels in three phases: CAPTURE (window → document → ... → target's parent), TARGET (handlers on the target itself), BUBBLE (parent → ... → document → window). addEventListener's third argument picks the leg: true/`{capture: true}` runs on capture, default runs on bubble. stopPropagation() halts further nodes from seeing it; stopImmediatePropagation also cancels same-element handlers; preventDefault cancels the browser's default action (a separate thing entirely). Delegation relies on the bubble leg.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C[capture: window → ... → parent] --> T[target phase]
    T --> B[bubble: parent → ... → window]
    SP[stopPropagation] -.cuts.-> B
    SI[stopImmediatePropagation] -.also cuts same-element.-> B
    PD[preventDefault] --> D[cancels browser default — separate axis]
    PA[passive: true] --> SC[scroll not blocked — perf contract]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why capture exists (the design reasoning): before bubbling, only capture existed (Netscape); Microsoft pushed bubbling; the DOM standard kept BOTH legs so either direction could intercept. The practical modern use of capture: interception BEFORE target handlers run — a capture listener on document/window sees a click before the target can stopPropagation it (the pattern for global analytics, hotkeys that must outrank page handlers, and security wrappers that must observe even stopped events). stopPropagation on the capture leg can prevent the click from EVER reaching the target — how focus-lock and modal-trap implementations work.

The passive-listener contract (the perf mechanism worth naming): for touchmove/wheel, the browser must know BEFORE running your handler whether preventDefault might be called — if it might, it must delay scrolling until your handler finishes (jank on every scroll). passive: true declares 'never preventDefault' up front, so scrolling proceeds on the compositor thread without waiting for JS. The history: Chrome made touchstart/wheel listeners passive BY DEFAULT on document-level targets (2017) precisely because missing passive was the top scroll-jank cause — know your listener flags, they're performance contracts.

The event-object lifecycle (the completeness corner): the event object is pooled/recycled in some engines after dispatch (IE) — never retain it; copy what you need (event.target, coordinates) synchronously. event.target (the deepest node actually clicked) vs event.currentTarget (the node the handler is ON — changes through propagation, equals 'this' in the handler) — the pair you use in every delegated handler to distinguish 'what was clicked' from 'where I'm listening'.
